teach.title: What it does

notice.ask: Tap the verb in the opening clause of each sentence. What do the two endings have in common?

teach.say: Latin marks an action finished before another future one with **the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)**. English says 'when I come to Rome, I shall see you'; Latin says *cum Rōmam vēnerō* — when I shall have come. When a clause opens with *cum, sī, ubi, postquam, antequam* and the main verb is future, expect this tense.

check.ask: gaudēbimus is future. Does vēnerit happen before it, or after?

teach.title: The singular: perfect stem + -erō, -eris, -erit
teach.say: Take the perfect stem — the third principal part without its *-ī* (*parāvī → parāv-*, *fēcī → fēc-*) — and add **-erō** for 'I', **-eris** for 'you', **-erit** for 'he, she, it'. The *i* of *-eris* is short.

check.ask: Fill the three singular future perfect forms of laudō.

teach.title: The plural: -erimus, -eritis, -erint
teach.say: The plural is built on the same perfect stem: **-erimus** for 'we', **-eritis** for 'you', **-erint** for 'they'. So *surgō* gives *surrēxerimus, surrēxeritis, surrēxerint*. Six endings, one stem, nothing else changes.

check.ask: Now the three plural future perfect forms of laudō.

teach.title: Not the plain perfect
teach.say: One syllable separates the two tenses. *lēgit* is the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense) and means 'he read'; *lēgerit* has *-eri-* before the ending and means 'he will have read'. The same goes for *vēnit / vēnerit* and *fēcit / fēcerit*. If the main verb is future, read the *-eri-* form as a future perfect.

check.ask: Which tense and mood is fēceris — the plain perfect, or the future perfect?

teach.title: Where it turns up
teach.say: This tense lives almost entirely in the clause that comes first. Open with *cum, sī, nisi, ubi, postquam* or *antequam*, keep the main verb in the plain future, and the first verb goes into the future perfect: *postquam omnēs surrēxerint, servī mēnsam movēbunt*. English uses a present or a perfect there and sounds no different.

check.ask: Cum opens the clause and quiēscēmus is future. Which tense is vēnerimus?

teach.title: Use it
teach.say: Put the finished action into the future perfect and leave the main verb in the plain future: *Sī Dāvus fūgerit, dominus eum quaeret* — if Davus runs away, his master will look for him. A passive verb uses two words, the perfect participle (a verb used like an adjective) with the future of *sum*: *epistula scrīpta erit*.

check.ask: Put occidō into the future perfect.

core.text: Latin marks an action finished before another future action with **the future perfect (the 'will have done' tense)**. Latin uses it in *sī* (if), *cum* (when), *postquam* (after) clauses: *cum vēnerō, gaudēbō* — when I have come, I will be glad. Forms: perfect stem + *-erō, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint*; passive: perfect participle + *erō, eris, erit* (*captus erit*). Latin name: *futūrum exāctum*.
English: *by noon he will have left*. In *if* and *when* clauses English drops it — *when you have finished, call me* — but the logic is the same.
Perfect stem + -erō … -erint. In a sī / cum / postquam clause with a future main verb translate it as a plain present or perfect: sī vēnerit = if he comes.

invented.en: If you write the letter, I will be glad.
When we have had dinner, we will sleep.

core.text: The perfect subjunctive (the 'have done' form: nescio quid fecerit; ne timueris = don't be afraid) has the same endings except *-erō* / *-erim*. The job decides: in a sī / cum / postquam clause pointing to the future it is the future perfect (*sī vēnerit, gaudēbō*); after *nē* (don't) or a question word it is the perfect subjunctive (*nē timuerīs*).

more.text: Also easy to confuse: the perfect (the 'did / has done' tense) ends *-ērunt* in the plural, the future perfect *-erint* — *vēnērunt* they came, *vēnerint* they will have come. The third person plural is the one place the two nearly touch.

The learner's notes: the future perfect is an action viewed as completed in the future; in English 'will have' + past participle. Latin builds the active from the 2nd stem + *-er-* + endings, with *-int* rather than *-unt* in the third plural precisely to keep it apart from the perfect; the passive is the perfect participle + *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt* (*captus erō*, *captī erunt*). Latin uses it freely in subordinate clauses where English has the present or perfect: *quī vīderit, crēdet* — he who has seen will believe.

Ørberg's chapter 30: *dux mīlitem laudābit, sī fortiter pugnāverit*; *discipulus laudābitur sī magistrō pāruerit et industrius fuerit*; passive *pater gaudēbit sī fīlius laudātus erit*. Irregulars follow the perfect stem: *fuerō, potuerō, voluerō, ierō*. In a main clause on its own it is rare and means a confident 'will have': *vīderimus*, we will have seen. With *cum* it stays in the indicative (the plain statement form) because it is a real future time, not story background (compare cum + subjunctive, Week 6).
Latin is strict where English is lazy: where English lets a present ('when I come') stand for a finished future action, Latin insists on the future perfect.
